headline: High: shared git/workspace and broad write access create dangerous default conflict and data-flow risks between Aider and Continue.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider reads and writes git-tracked files and Continue reads/writes workspace files, so either agent can ingest the other’s output through the shared repo/editor surface. Continue’s MCP/tooling path can also be influenced by file content if the operator routes it there. This is not provably blocked, but it is not a direct shared channel by default.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or workspace directory
IF one agent’s generated text is later opened by the other as source material
mitigations: Separate the agents into different repos or worktrees
Disable automatic ingestion of generated files
Review any file before passing it between agents
Use read-only mode for one agent during handoff
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to agent-generated files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Aider touches source code and git history, while Continue touches source code and open editor buffers. In a shared workspace, either agent can expose sensitive code or secrets present in files to the other through the common filesystem. Both also have broad model-provider egress, so file contents may leave the host during normal use.
conditions: IF sensitive code, credentials, or secrets are present in the shared workspace
IF either agent sends file contents to its configured model provider
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared repo and editor buffers
Use separate workspaces for each agent
Turn off network access for one agent during sensitive edits
Redact secrets before opening files in either agent
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Aider can write the filesystem and modify git state; Continue can also write the filesystem and shares state via filesystem. In the same repo, concurrent edits can race on files and git history without a documented locking mechanism, making destructive overwrite or conflicting commits plausible in default use.
conditions: IF both agents edit the same files or branch concurrently
IF no external lock or merge discipline is enforced
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate branch
Pause one agent while the other writes
Run git status before every handoff
Use file-level ownership conventions
requires-engineering: add locking around shared repo writes

D_cascading_error.rationale: Aider produces code edits and git commits that Continue can read from the shared workspace. Continue may then treat those outputs as authoritative context for further edits or tool calls. Because Continue’s tool use requires user approval, the cascade is mitigated but still exists in default workflows.
conditions: IF Continue consumes Aider-generated patches or commits as trusted context
IF the operator approves downstream tool calls without independent verification
mitigations: Require a human review step between agents
Compare diffs before approving any follow-up action
Limit Continue to read-only analysis after Aider edits
Use explicit task boundaries for each agent
requires-engineering: add verification of Aider outputs before Continue acts

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents are open-source coding tools with similar data classes and no stated residency or certification mismatch, so no clear compliance breach is evidenced. The main compliance risk is local handling of source code and secrets, which is shared rather than divergent; the other agent is not separately implicated beyond the same workspace.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is placed into the shared workspace
IF the operator relies on an unstated residency or retention guarantee
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in the shared repo
Confirm provider and workspace retention settings
Use separate environments for regulated projects
Document data-handling expectations before use
requires-engineering: implement policy-based workspace segregation
